entries.summary: AI agents rebuilt a .NET MAUI app with platform UI in days. See what that cost to build, what it costs to maintain, and what changed at runtime, so you can weigh the same choice for your app.
entries.text: How you build a cross-platform app has always come down to a few hard constraints. Over the years I’ve talked with a lot of teams about how they chose their approach, and the factors are consistent: what the team already knows, how many codebases it has the capacity to support, what it costs to build and to maintain, solution characteristics like app size and performance, and the health of the ecosystem and support behind the stack. Many of you reevaluate your technology investment choice on at least an annual basis. In 2026 there’s a major new factor to consider: AI coding agents. Today the first two factors, team knowledge and team capacity, look different. A well-configured GitHub Copilot can write UIKit or Android Views whether or not anyone on your team has, and it doesn’t mind writing the same screen twice. Does that flatten the playing field between fully cross-platform and fully platform-specific, or is there still value in choosing a single stack to reach multiple platforms? I ran an experiment to find out. The short version: agents made a second UI cheap to build, but owning it still took work. The first pass of a full rewrite took under four hours of my time. Adding the same feature to both versions used more worker model time with two UIs, and the coordinating agent used more model time than both implementation groups combined. The experiment Barista Notes is a .NET MAUI app that runs on Android, iOS, macOS, and Windows. It has a dozen screens, more than 20 NuGet
entries.title: AI is Changing the Cross-Platform Decision Matrix

entries.summary: Stage and validate packages privately on NuGet.org, then approve their release when you are ready. The post Introducing staged publishing on NuGet.org appeared first on .NET Blog.
entries.text: A successful build tells you that your pipeline finished. It does not tell you that you meant to release. Today, we are introducing staged publishing on NuGet.org, available to all package publishers, so you can prepare and validate packages privately before making an explicit decision to publish them. Upload a security fix ahead of its coordinated disclosure. Gather the packages for a feature release without exposing an unfinished set. Let automation prepare a large update, then review it on NuGet.org before it reaches the people who depend on it. Your pipeline prepares the release. You decide when it goes live. A release boundary you control With a normal package push, upload starts the public publishing process. Staged publishing adds a place to stop: the package goes through NuGet.org validation, but stays private until an authorized maintainer promotes it through the website. That gives you time to review what you are about to ship, fix validation problems, and choose the release moment. Staging is opt-in. Existing dotnet nuget push workflows continue to work. You can adopt staging for a security-sensitive package or a coordinated release without changing every publishing workflow at once. Staging also differs from unlisting. An unlisted package can still be restored by its exact version. A staged package is not available to consumers at all. entries.summary: .NET 11 is here with C# 15, faster developer tools, runtime and library improvements, and new capabilities for web, mobile, desktop, and AI apps.
entries.text: Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities. Download .NET 11 .NET 11 support .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support (STS) release with two years of support under the .NET support policy. STS and Long Term Support (LTS) releases have the same quality and servicing policies; the difference is the length of support. .NET 10 remains a supported LTS option. Stay current with servicing updates whichever release you choose. Join us at .NET Conf, November 10-13 Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026. The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions. Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote, or browse the conference session playlist. entries.summary: Take the 2026 .NET Developer Survey to share your experience, help identify common challenges, and guide future .NET investments.
entries.text: It’s that time of the year! The 2026 .NET Developer Survey is open, and we’d love to hear about your experience. The survey takes about 15 minutes to complete, and your feedback helps the .NET team understand where to invest next. Take the 2026 .NET Developer Survey As a thank you for your time, eligible U.S. residents who complete the survey and leave their email address at the end can enter for a chance to win .NET swag! Your feedback helps us build a better .NET We want to understand what it’s like to use .NET in your everyday work. Where does it make things easier? What’s harder than it should be? Your answers help us understand how you use .NET and what would make it work better for you. Hearing from more developers helps us see which challenges are widely shared, including ones that might not come up in GitHub issues or community conversations. You don’t need to be using the latest release to contribute. Maintaining an older application is just as much a part of .NET development as starting a new project, and we want that experience reflected in the feedback. A thank you for participating Eligible U.S. residents can enter a sweepstakes for a chance to win one of 10 .NET branded swag packages, each with an approximate retail value of $15 USD. To enter, complete the survey and provide your email address when prompted at the end. Ten winners will be selected at random and notified at the email address they provided. entries.summary: Modernize your .NET apps for Windows Arm64 with the GitHub Copilot upgrade agent, from identifying migration blockers to planning and making code changes.
entries.text: Arm64 offers the potential for lower compute costs and more efficient infrastructure. But what would it take to get your existing .NET application running on it? The answer may be scattered across your code, dependencies, and build settings. You need to know what already supports Arm64, what needs updating, and how much work is involved. Finding those answers by hand can become a project of its own. The GitHub Copilot upgrade agent helps you move from those questions to concrete changes. It assesses your .NET projects for migration from Windows x64 or x86 to Windows Arm64, identifies blockers, creates a migration plan, and helps update your code, dependencies, and configuration. https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/wp-content/uploads/sites/10/2026/11/arm64-modernization.webm Understand what is blocking your migration An x64 build setting is easy to spot. A package that quietly depends on a native library without an Arm64 binary can take more digging. Before you migrate, you need to know where those assumptions show up in your application. Common blockers include: Code and build settings tied to a specific architecture Native dependencies that do not provide Arm64 binaries Packages or libraries that need versions compatible with Arm64 Platform assumptions spread across multiple projects Configuration that targets only x64 or x86 environments The upgrade agent helps with that investigation, assessing your .NET projects and identifying the work needed to move from Windows x64 o
entries.title: Modernize your .NET apps for Windows Arm64 with GitHub Copilot

entries.summary: Agent skills can be delivered in NuGet packages as a way to deliver up-to-date library documentation to models. The post Delivering Skills in NuGet packages appeared first on .NET Blog.
entries.text: Agent skills were introduced by Anthropic in 2025 and have quickly become commonplace for AI-driven development. dotnet/skills and Impeccable skills are good examples. Agent skills are typically distributed via git repos. We’ve been working on skill delivery via NuGet packages and found that the approach can be effective. The common thread is that repos and packages are units of development that can be used as distribution vehicles for skills. Skills solve two main problems: fill in gaps in model knowledge and can prescribe “our way” of approaching a task. New NuGet packages will always be ahead of model training and can benefit from just-in-time skill delivery. Here’s a quick demo using the markout package, whch contains a set of skills: $ dotnet-inspect package markout -S Skills path size skills/markout-built-in-shapes/SKILL.md 9457 skills/markout-composite-cells-cards/SKILL.md 6764 skills/markout-conditional-composition/SKILL.md 4978 skills/markout-output-formats/SKILL.md 7744 skills/markout/SKILL.md 8551 Baseline We’ve done a lot of experimentation. We’ve found that agents (as a baseline behavior) are capable of finding content in the NuGet cache to learn about a package. This includes reading README.md files and even writing throwaway programs that reflect over assembly metadata. entries.summary: Microsoft and Syncfusion are collaborating on Blazor through a free, open-source component toolkit, framework contributions, and developer tooling.
entries.text: We’re pleased to announce our collaboration with Syncfusion to advance Blazor! Syncfusion has released a free, open-source toolkit of Blazor components, and its engineers have contributed fixes and tests to ASP.NET Core and the .NET scaffolding tools. Their investment helps developers building with the toolkit and strengthens the platform for the entire Blazor community. This collaboration builds on Syncfusion’s contributions to .NET MAUI, where Syncfusion released an open-source toolkit and committed engineering resources to the framework itself. We’re excited to see that commitment extend to Blazor. Introducing the Syncfusion Toolkit for Blazor The Syncfusion Toolkit for Blazor provides reusable UI components for Blazor apps under the MIT license. The toolkit includes charts, buttons, calendars, date and time pickers, text and numeric inputs, dialogs, tooltips, and loading indicators. Syncfusion Toolkit for Blazor showcase featuring charts and input controls in desktop and mobile layouts. The toolkit is free for everyone, including commercial use. It doesn’t require a license key or eligibility for Syncfusion’s Community License. The open-source toolkit is separate from the broader commercial Syncfusion Blazor suite, which includes additional components and features. You can explore the code, samples, and contribution guidance in the Syncfusion Blazor Toolkit repository. entries.title: Blazor Welcomes Open-Source Contributions from Syncfusion

entries.summary: Microsoft and Infragistics are collaborating on Blazor through free, open-source components, new .NET 11 analyzers, and developer tooling.
entries.text: We’re pleased to welcome Infragistics as an active contributor to Blazor! As part of our collaboration, Infragistics has made more than 50 of its Blazor controls free and open source, and its engineers are contributing directly to the framework. Their work includes new Blazor analyzers for .NET 11 and tooling to help you get started with their components. Infragistics recently announced this collaboration, building on its experience developing UI components for .NET. By investing in both open-source components and Blazor itself, Infragistics is helping improve the experience for every Blazor developer, whether or not you use its controls. Free, open-source Blazor components The Ignite UI for Blazor open-source components include inputs, navigation, and layout controls such as Combo Box, Date Picker, Tree, Stepper, and Tile Manager. Grid Lite provides a lightweight option for displaying tabular data. A team directory built with Ignite UI for Blazor Grid Lite, showing column filters and custom cell content. These components are available under the MIT license for use in personal and commercial applications. You can inspect the source, report issues, and contribute improvements in the Ignite UI for Blazor repository. This is a free, open-source subset of the broader Ignite UI for Blazor offering, not a trial of the commercial suite.
